coverage.assessment: Milnes's praise of Swinburne's unpublished poetry is no longer paid off by the ballad recitation. The reason Adams fails the Hugo test (no ear, no command of the language) is cut. 'The worst liars were the candid' arrives without its premise. Every other essential chain survives: army impulse, father's argument, affidavits, Butler quarrel, Cambridge House invitations.

'The three young men' now has two members, Oliphant and Stirling, whose ages and later fates are dropped, so only Swinburne's drift is shown. The staircase, receiving line and bedroom-candle scene remain spatially clear.

The Minister's curt line, the footman's escalating calls, Palmerston's 'Ha! ... Ha!', Stirling's verdict and Milnes's Hugo anecdote all keep their speakers and turn-taking. Thackeray's reproach is reasonably summarized.

The Butler hedges survive ('Perhaps he was right', 'for some reason', 'at least, not then'). The opening loses the unanimity clause ('no one doubted it') and the secretary's own charge against Russell's replies. This softens the 1862 certainty that later chapters overturn.
Retrospective markers survive: 'afterwards he felt less sure', Thackeray's 'last time' before 1863, 'Ten years afterwards'. Nothing anticipates the archival vindication of Palmerston.
Two periodic, self-deflating passages are flattened: the tearful 'facing friends' sentence and the Cambridge House catalogue of dull guests. The aphorisms and verbatim lines are intact.

The son's 'nothing to choose' between Palmerston and Russell loses its framing: the hesitation over whose word to trust, and the note that Englishmen saw little difference. The theme of friends drifting apart thins to one figure.

Milnes's warmth (to 013) is intact. The Palmerston puzzle (to 012) is intact locally and its apology endpoint survives. The Swinburne gulf survives locally, but the 023 revision cut the Swinburne recall.

dependencies.assessment: The local text keeps Milnes's kindness, the charity, Adams's gratitude and the club proposal. Chapter 013's revision keeps the embrace and 'his young American friend'.

evidence.quote: Milnes made it his business to be kind.
Immediately afterwards Milnes proposed Henry Adams for membership
with a whoop of triumph he rushed to throw both arms about his neck and kiss him on both cheeks

dependencies.assessment: The puzzle stays open locally and nothing anticipates the apology. Chapter 012's revision keeps the 'beg his pardon' endpoint but cut 'He surprised the Minister by refusing to pursue his attack on General Butler'. The explicit Butler echo therefore weakens; that is a neighbor issue, not chargeable here.

evidence.quote: Palmerston wanted a quarrel; the motive seemed evident; yet when the quarrel was made, he backed out of it
he was obliged at last to admit himself in error, and to consent in spirit
He surprised the Minister by refusing to pursue his attack on General Butler.

dependencies.assessment: The local gulf is well preserved ('alone was tame', 'only receive', 'worm'). Chapter 023's revision removed the clause recalling Swinburne and Stevenson, so the Anglo-American echo no longer reaches back to this chapter. A planning gap in 023 is likely.

evidence.quote: but one could only receive; one had nothing to give--nothing even to offer.
he had felt it when he was with Swinburne, and, again, with Robert Louis Stevenson
The American felt that the defect, if defect it were, was in himself; but he did not carry self-abasement

findings.claim: Milnes's hint that Swinburne had written unpublished poetry 'of really extraordinary merit' is kept. The revision then cuts the only demonstration of it: the declaimed unpublished ballads 'as though they were books of the Iliad'. Paragraph 18 still says Swinburne united the others 'by his humor even more than by his poetry'.
findings.counterevidence: Stirling's bedtime request for 'Queen Rosamund' implies interest in the poetry.

evidence.quote: They knew not what to make of his rhetorical recitation of his own unpublished ballads
They knew not what to make of his rhetorical recitation of his own unpublished ballads, which he declaimed as though they were books of the Iliad.
Milnes lingered in Adams's room to add that Swinburne had written some poetry, not yet published, of really extraordinary merit.
Swinburne was millions of ages far from them, yet he united them by his humor even more than by his poetry.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's ballads sentence before 'Swinburne was millions of ages far from them'.
findings.plan_relation: Required: the plan lists Swinburne's dazzling monologue as essential.
findings.reader_effect: The setup loses its payoff. The comparison of humor with poetry refers to poetry the reader never witnesses, and the bedroom monologue shrinks to feats of memory.
findings.title: Swinburne's own poetry is promised but never shown

findings.claim: The revision cuts two sentences. The first ('Adams had neither') explains the Hugo failure by ear and language. The second ('Only in France is the attitude of prayer possible') is the frame that 'With the best of will, one could not do this in London' answers. The first draft had already dropped the object of 'almost as helpless' (an American private secretary), so the comparison now dangles.
findings.counterevidence: 'Adams's failure was equally gross' and V8 still signal failure, and 'the Boston mind' gives a partial reason.

evidence.quote: Only in France is the attitude of prayer possible; in England it became absurd.
was almost as helpless as an American private secretary in personal contact with them
Appreciating French verse requires extraordinary knowledge of the language and rare refinement of ear, and Adams had neither.
Swinburne tested him then and there by one of his favorite tests--Victor Hugo. Adams tried to evade Swinburne's vehement insistence
Even Monckton Milnes, who felt the splendors of Hugo and Landor, was almost as helpless in personal contact with them.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore 'and Adams had neither' (with its clause) and the 'Only in France' sentence. Add 'as an American private secretary' after 'almost as helpless'.
findings.plan_relation: Required: the Hugo/Landor tests and Milnes's anecdote are essential.
findings.reader_effect: Adams's failure becomes mere evasion rather than self-condemning incapacity. Milnes's Hugo story reads as a detached anecdote rather than an illustration of worship possible in France and absurd in England.
findings.title: Hugo test and Milnes anecdote lose their explanation and frame

findings.claim: The revision cuts two framing sentences. One is the hesitation 'between Palmerston's word and Russell's word' that gave years of education. The other is the opening of paragraph 11 on Palmerston as Prime Minister meddling in foreign affairs while diplomats court Russell. The first draft had already removed 'Englishmen saw little difference between them' and the premise of 'The worst liars were the candid'.
findings.counterevidence: Chapter 010 establishes Russell as Foreign Secretary, and the contrast itself is stated in paragraph 11.

evidence.quote: between Palmerston's word and Russell's word, one hesitated to decide, and gave years of education to deciding, whether either could be trusted, or how far.
Englishmen saw little difference between them, and Americans were bound to follow English experience in English character.
Between Palmerston's word and Russell's word, one hesitated to decide, and gave years of education to deciding
No professional diplomatists worried about falsehoods. The worst liars were the candid.
His son, being young and ill-balanced in temper, thought there was nothing to choose.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's 'Between Palmerston's word and Russell's word...' sentence in paragraph 7.
findings.plan_relation: Required: Minister Adams trusts Russell, the son sees no difference.
findings.reader_effect: The son's 'nothing to choose' and the Minister's preference for Russell, an essential contrast that later chapters overturn, now arrive with little argumentative ground. The Queen's memorandum sentence floats without the trust question it served.
findings.title: Palmerston-versus-Russell trust question loses its framing

findings.claim: The revision cuts the clause about being 'exasperated, furious, bitter, and choking with tears' and the 'pillow' sentence. Paragraph 3 now jumps from the need to 'affect candor' straight to the Times read over the muffin.
findings.counterevidence: V2 and the muffin and 'licking' details survive.

evidence.quote: not always a simple act when one is exasperated, furious, bitter, and choking with tears over the blunders and incapacity of one's Government
If one shed tears, they must be shed on one's pillow.
therefore they must affect candor. One must read one's Times every morning over one's muffin without reading aloud

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's two sentences ('That is not always a simple act...'; 'If one shed tears...').
findings.reader_effect: The aphorism that self-restraint among friends is harder than before enemies loses the private anguish that motivates it. The semicolon-built crescendo of the chapter's title idea is flattened.
findings.title: The emotional cost of 'facing friends' is removed

findings.claim: The first draft dropped Oliphant's age ('a man of thirty or thereabouts') and Adams's 'desperate' wish for friends. The revision then cuts the later fates of Oliphant and Stirling. 'The three young men... each went his own way' is followed only by Swinburne's story.
findings.counterevidence: Swinburne is described as 'a boy', and the Milnes quip still carries the theme.

evidence.quote: The third was a man of thirty or thereabouts
Oliphant he met oftener; all the world knew and loved him; but he too disappeared in the way that all the world knows.
Oliphant too disappeared in the way that all the world knows. Stirling of Keir passed from Adams's vision into Sir William Stirling-Maxwell.
The three young men returned to London, and each went his own way.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's Oliphant and Stirling sentences and add 'a man of thirty or thereabouts' to Oliphant's introduction.
findings.reader_effect: Readers cannot readily identify the trio, and the essential motif of friends drifting apart, which links to Milnes's 'losing friends', is reduced to a single figure.
findings.title: 'Three young men' and the friends' drifting apart are left half-told

findings.claim: The revision removes the catalogue of dull, unfashionable guests. 'Lady Palmerston was no longer young or handsome' now leads straight to 'Yet, beyond a doubt'. The first draft had already trimmed the periodic semicolon series.
findings.counterevidence: 'sympathique' and 'The world never explains such riddles' survive.

evidence.quote: the women were of course ill-dressed and middle-aged; the men looked mostly bored or out of place; yet, beyond a doubt, Cambridge House was the best
The people one met there were never smart and seldom young.
Lady Palmerston was no longer young or handsome. Yet, beyond a doubt, Cambridge House was the best, and perhaps the only political house in London.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore one clause: 'The women were of course ill-dressed and middle-aged, and the men looked mostly bored or out of place.'
findings.plan_relation: Optional tradeoff within an essential section.
findings.reader_effect: The 'riddle' of the house's inexplicable success is asserted rather than built, and the narrator's comic deflation is lost.
findings.title: Cambridge House riddle stripped of its evidence

findings.claim: The revision drops 'He could see it; the Legation knew it; no one doubted it' and the young secretary's judgment that Russell's replies were 'insolent in their disregard of truth'. What remains is others' gossip that Russell lied.
findings.counterevidence: 'The intensity of the private secretary's rage sprang from his belief' keeps his conviction.

evidence.quote: He could see it; the Legation knew it; no one doubted it; no one thought of questioning it.
To an irritable young private secretary of twenty-four, they were insolent in their disregard of truth.
Every day the British Government deliberately crowded him one step further into the grave. The Trent Affair showed where Palmerston and Russell stood.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore 'He could see it; the Legation knew it; no one doubted it.'
findings.reader_effect: The confident 1862 theory that chapter 012 later dismantles is slightly less the young man's own conviction.
findings.title: Opening rage loses its unanimity and the secretary's own charge

strengths: The footman sequence keeps its full Handrew–Hanthony–Halexander escalation, so V4 lands.
The Butler episode keeps the Minister's curt line, the loss of the Cambridge House invitations and the unresolved closing question without premature vindication.
Thackeray's wrong-house setup is brief and correctly framed as the 'last time' before his 1863 death, ending on V3's dash rhythm.
The Fryston arc keeps Milnes's patronage, the bedroom monologue, Stirling's candle-lit verdict and the 'getting on' irony.
Palmerston's mechanical laugh survives with its 'Yes! ... Yes!' gloss and the 1810 line.
